This workshop teaches the technical skills that modern empirical data analysis runs on – retrieving data from an online repository, working with code so that another person can reproduce your steps, committing to your analytical choices before you make them, and writing a report that carries its own code inside it. It teaches them through an applied 'replication' exercise rather than in the abstract.

Participants reproduce one of the reanalyses that made up the Multi100 project, whose results appeared in *Nature* (Aczel et al. 2026), then test the robustness of a published claim by the original author (OA) [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic]. You use the same data, the same tools and the same workflow the project itself used.

## You are the sixth analyst

The day centres on the EU-frames case, OA's 2016 study of how the EU was framed across 27 countries. Five analysts have already reanalysed its central claim for the Multi100 project, and their results are public. You become the sixth, and you work through the same moves a researcher actually makes:

1. **Reproduce a published analyst's result.** Take the analysis code as it was submitted to the Multi100 project, run it on the original data and land the exact coefficient it produced.
2. **See how an error entered real submitted code.** Your run reproduces the recorded value first time. A second number in the public trail does not match it, and the story behind that gap – a survey wave read twice, caught and corrected in the open – is told with the full OSF record on screen.
3. **State an estimand and draw the graph.** Say precisely which quantity the study is trying to estimate. That quantity is the estimand. Then draw the causal graph, a directed acyclic graph or DAG, that tells you which variables to adjust for.
4. **Preregister one specification, the way researchers do on OSF.** Pick one defensible analysis from a menu of choices, then write down what you expect in a shortened version of a real preregistration template, before you run anything.
5. **Run it and watch the class multiverse grow.** Submit your result and see it land on a live chart, next to your classmates' and the five published analysts'.
6. **Read a specification curve.** Work out what a thousand-plus results together can, and cannot, tell you.

The exercise is a miniature version of Multi100 itself: same claim, many analysts, explicit choices, comparable results.

## Two routes, one destination

Both routes cover every task, and both reach exactly the same numbers. Whichever you choose, you do the same analysis, and nobody misses anything by picking one over the other.

::: {.callout-tip}
### Route 1 – R and Positron (recommended)

Install R and the Positron editor once, before the day, then download a ready-made workspace – a single zip file holding the analysis code, the data and a report to fill in. There is nothing to configure and no account to create. You open the folder and start working. This is the closest to how the analysis is really done, and the workspace is yours to keep afterwards.

The [Setup](setup.qmd) page walks you through the installation in plain steps. Give yourself a little time before the day, depending on what you already have.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
### Route 2 – Browser lab (nothing to install)

Open the [Browser lab](exercise/browser-lab.qmd) page and everything runs inside the tab, on a version of R that lives in your web browser. Nothing to install, no account, and it works on a borrowed or locked-down machine. The page takes ten to thirty seconds to wake up the first time, so read the task while it warms. Every required task is here, at full parity with Route 1.
:::

You need no git, no GitHub account, no OSF account and no sign-ups for either route. If you would like to add version control and publishing to your toolkit later, the optional [Git and GitHub companion module](companion/git-github.qmd) shows you how, at your own pace.

## Four blocks, ninety minutes each

Two breaks and a lunch sit between the blocks. The callout above gives the clock times for the next delivery, and the lengths below hold whenever the course runs.

| Block | Length | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| Block 1 – "One paper, three verdicts" | 90 minutes | The three Rs (reproducibility, robustness, replicability) and the EU-frames case, ending with a first hands-on run of the constrained model. |
| Break | | |
| Block 2 – "The record's second number, then the question underneath" | 90 minutes | The story of the −3.853/−3.804 gap – a wave file read twice, caught and corrected in the open – then estimands and DAGs. |
| Lunch | | |
| Block 3 – "Preregister like an analyst" | 90 minutes | Completing a causal graph, choosing one analytical deviation from a specification menu, preregistering it, then running and submitting your own result. |
| Break | | |
| Block 4 – "Reading the multiverse" | 90 minutes | Reading the class's results against the full specification curve and the five published analysts, with an introduction to inference across a multiverse of results. |
